text: DevOps, Testing and Deployment already covered Dev, Test, and Production as a promotion pipeline for moving one change safely toward release. This lesson asks a bigger, rarer question: does this organization need more than one production instance in the first place?

Those are genuinely different questions. Having three Dev/Test/Prod tiers is normal for every organization on the platform. Having two separate Production instances — two places where real, live business actually runs — is a much bigger architectural decision, and it's almost never the right default.

Two real justifications show up repeatedly in actual enterprise implementations. First, a regulatory data-residency law that requires certain data to physically stay within a region, when the available instance regions can't satisfy that from one instance. Second, truly independent business units or subsidiaries with no operational need to share a customer record, a CMDB, or a service catalog — where forcing them onto one platform creates real friction and no real benefit.

The standard guidance still favors one production instance, using Domain Separation for multi-tenancy needs within it, because a second production instance multiplies real, ongoing cost. Every upgrade now happens twice, on two schedules. Every platform-wide security model has to be kept consistent across two instances instead of one. Every integration partner may need two endpoints. Every monitoring setup and on-call runbook exists twice, indefinitely.

Before recommending a second production instance, an architect's real job is to test whether the constraint is actually unavoidable. Does the law truly require physical regional separation, or would strong access controls inside one instance satisfy it? Does the subsidiary genuinely never need to share data with the parent? Only a confirmed 'yes, and no single instance can satisfy it' justifies the larger ongoing cost — otherwise, the default stays one instance.

One instance, used well, beats two instances maintained twice as hard. Next: Domain Separation — the real mechanism for multi-tenancy inside that single shared instance, and the complexity it genuinely adds to every customization going forward.
